response = "The first discrimination in a patient with unexplained iron overload is biochemical rather than clinical, and it begins with two tests that behave very differently. Transferrin saturation above 45 percent prompts further evaluation for iron overload, since a saturated transport protein points toward parenchymal loading; by contrast, serum ferritin is elevated in both inherited and acquired forms of iron overload, so a high value establishes that iron is in excess without identifying how it came to be there. Even though serum ferritin rises nonspecifically during systemic inflammation, a transferrin saturation above that 45 percent threshold remains reason enough to carry the workup forward. Where biochemistry raises the question, genotyping begins to answer it. That homozygosity for C282Y is the most common genotype in hereditary hemochromatosis indicates that the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Hereditary hemochromatosis follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, a mode of transmission that cannot be squared with the predominance of C282Y homozygotes among affected patients and that is equally irreconcilable with inheritance through paired alleles on an autosome. The family history is therefore read in the light of what an HFE genotype can and cannot account for. Mechanism and arithmetic separate the two etiologies further. Hepcidin deficiency increases intestinal iron absorption in HFE-related hemochromatosis. Iron in transfusional overload accumulates predominantly in reticuloendothelial macrophages. The acquired side has the advantage of being straightforwardly calculable. One unit of packed red blood cells contains approximately 200 to 250 milligrams of iron, and one unit of transfused packed red blood cells delivers approximately 25 milligrams of iron; those two accountings cannot both be correct, and it is the larger figure on which the arithmetic of chronic transfusion depends, since a patient receiving two units a month accrues grams of iron each year against negligible excretion. What finally settles the attribution is direct evidence from the liver itself. MRI R2* imaging quantifies liver iron concentration without biopsy. Perls' Prussian blue staining demonstrates the cellular distribution of iron in liver tissue. Sequence matters in applying that evidence: hepatic iron is measured before any depletive therapy is begun, and the iron carried in every unit of blood is the reason that a patient whose anemia requires continued transfusion must have iron removed pharmacologically rather than by bleeding. Therapeutic phlebotomy is the first-line treatment for hereditary hemochromatosis. Iron chelation therapy is used for transfusion-dependent patients with iron overload."
